newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel head says budget deficit worrying.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel head says budget deficit worrying.

text.p: Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel said on Sunday that the 1997 budget deficit was already causing him deep concern and demanded immediate action.
"The central problem of the economy today is a problem of the budget," Frenkel told a business conference.
He said the January deficit, which the Treasury earlier reported was 1.28 billion shekels, was too big to delay taking measures until April, as Treasury officials have been saying.

"The Bank of Israel proposes operative instruments that will monitor the budget on a month-to-month basis," he said. "Why wait until April? We're in February and we can already see we have a very big problem."
Frenkel launched a defence of the Bank of Israel's monetary policy, which has been widely criticised for allegedly causing slower economic growth and exchange rate problems.
Frenkel said if the bank had not kept to its restrictive policy, inflation would be now considerably higher and Israel's standing in international financial markets would be poorer.

Israel's consumer price index slowed from a 14.6 percent annualised rate in first-half 1996 to less than half that in the second part of the year. Frenkel noted that the decline came despite an ever-widening budget deficit over the year.

Frenkel noted that short-term interest rates had fallen nearly three percentage points since the middle of 1996, despite the fact that the government's planned budget reductions for 1997 had not yet been implemented.

Although the Bank of Israel has been forced to inject large amounts of money into the economy to support the exchange rate in recent weeks, Frenkel said the central bank had the liquidity situation under control.

Treasury officials estimate the bank has spent in excess of $1 billion since the beginning of the year in a bid to keep the shekel rate against the official basket of currencies from falling below its official trading band.
"In contrast to claims the Bank of Israel has lost control...this simply has not happened," Frenkel said, noting there was no pressure in the market for interest rates to fall.
Frenkel stressed that the foreign currency that the Bank of Israel has been buying is being invested and constituted a source of income for the central bank.

He downplayed the role high interest rates have played in spurring capital inflows. Although high interest rates have caused domestic borrowers to take cheaper foreign currency loans, Frenkel noted that $4.7 billion had flowed into Israel in the last two years from direct investment.
He termed the big increase in direct investment a vote of confidence in the Israeli economy.
